Mnemonic: Hebrew simply DROPS 'am/is/are'. "I am tired" = Ani ayef — literally "I tired." Think of li-HIOT as a verb that takes a HIatus in the present.
Example (English): I want to be a doctor.

Mnemonic: ya-CHOL = "Ya, cool!" — Yes, I can, no problem.
Example (English): I can't come tomorrow.

Mnemonic: roh-TSEH — a waiter leans in: "Rotze?" Just ROT-SAY what you want.
Example (English): What do you want to drink?

Mnemonic: tsa-REECH — you need to be RICH to afford it. (Tzarich also means "must".)
Example (English): I need a new key.

Mnemonic: OH-seh — "Oh, say…" Ma ata ose? ("What are you doing?") is the most-used question in Israel.
Example (English): What are you doing now?

Mnemonic: DOV — a bear is big enough to eat a DOVE in one bite. (Handy: the two are almost the same sound — dov / yona.)
Example (English): The bear is big and strong.

Mnemonic: PAR — a bull runs at PAR speed. Note pair: par (bull) / para (cow) — just add the -a for female.
Example (English): The bull runs in the field.

Mnemonic: pa-RA — the cow says "pa-RAAA" instead of moo. The Red Heifer of the Torah is the Para Aduma.
Example (English): The cow gives milk.

Mnemonic: cha-MOR — the donkey wants CHA-MORE hay. Calling someone a chamor is a classic Israeli insult.
Example (English): The donkey carries a heavy load.

Mnemonic: KOF — a monkey with a COUGH. Also the name of the Hebrew letter ק.
Example (English): The monkey eats a banana at the zoo.

Mnemonic: ga-DOL — Goliath (Golyat) was gadol. Also the root of ligdol, "to grow".
Example (Hebrew): יֵשׁ לָהֶם בַּיִת גָּדוֹל עִם גִּנָּה.
Example (translit): Yesh lahem bayit gadol im gina.
Example (English): They have a big house with a garden.

Mnemonic: a-ROCH — think of a long ARCH stretching away. Orech = length.
Example (English): The road is long but beautiful.

Mnemonic: ka-TSAR — a short haircut, like a CUT-SIR. From liktzor, to cut short/harvest.
Example (English): The story is short and interesting.

Mnemonic: ga-VO-ha — say it and your voice goes UP on the -VO-. Gova = height.
Example (English): My brother is taller than me.

Mnemonic: na-MOOCH — "not MUCH" of it. The opposite of gavoha, and used for prices and volume too.
Example (English): The table is too low.

Mnemonic: sha-FAN — a rabbit is a big FAN of carrots. (Shafan also means "coward" in slang.)
Example (English): The rabbit eats a carrot.

Mnemonic: ach-BAR — a mouse sneaking into the BAR. Also the word for a computer mouse.
Example (English): There's a mouse in the kitchen!

Mnemonic: na-CHASH — hear the hiss in the -CHASH. The serpent in Eden is Ha-Nachash.
Example (English): The snake is very dangerous.

Mnemonic: TSAV — short and squat, like the turtle itself. Sounds like "tsov" — slow.
Example (English): The turtle walks very slowly.

Mnemonic: a-ka-VEESH — "a-ka-VEESH" sounds like a web being spun. Kurei akavish = a spider's web.
Example (English): There's a big spider in the corner.

Mnemonic: ho-LECH — imagine walking and calling "Hoe! Lech!" Also: Yalla, lech! = "Come on, go!"
Example (English): I walk to work on foot.

Mnemonic: BA — a sheep goes "baa" as it comes toward you. Two letters, easiest verb in Hebrew.
Example (English): The guests are coming at six.

Mnemonic: yo-TZEH — the EXIT sign at every Israeli mall says יְצִיאָה (yetzia). "Yo, TSAY goodbye, I'm out."
Example (English): We leave the house at eight.

Mnemonic: cho-ZER — you return to ZERO, back to the start.
Example (English): He's coming back from the trip tomorrow.

Mnemonic: no-SEH-a — you travel by NOSE-ing the car forward. Use this for cars/buses; holech is on foot.
Example (English): We're traveling to Jerusalem by bus.

Mnemonic: par-PAR — say it twice like the two flapping wings: par-par, par-par.
Example (English): The butterfly is colorful and beautiful.

Mnemonic: ZVOOV — it literally buzzes: zvoov-zvoov.
Example (English): The fly is annoying me.

Mnemonic: CHEH-rek — a bug that wrecks your picnic. Juk is the everyday slang word for a cockroach.
Example (English): There are a lot of insects in the garden.

Mnemonic: go-ZAL — a fluffy chick that GOES ALL over the place. Israelis call a cute kid a gozal.
Example (English): The chick falls from the nest.

Mnemonic: tar-ne-GOL — a rooster crowing a long "tar-ne-GOOOL" at dawn. The -et ending makes it the hen.
Example (English): The rooster crows in the morning.

Mnemonic: ma-CHAR — "MY CAR is coming tomorrow." Machrataim = the day after tomorrow.
Example (English): Tomorrow I'm meeting the doctor.

Mnemonic: et-MOL — "et" (time) + a mumble. Shilshom = the day before yesterday.
Example (English): Yesterday it was very hot.

Mnemonic: AZ — two letters. Israelis open half their sentences with "Az…" the way English speakers say "So…"
Example (English): So what did you do?

Mnemonic: a-DA-yin — "Are we there yet? A-DYIN' to know." Od is the shorter, more casual alternative.
Example (English): I'm still studying Hebrew.

Mnemonic: PA-am — "Pa'am" alone means "once, back in the day". Kama pe'amim? = "How many times?"
Example (English): I've been there three times.

Mnemonic: yo-NA — Jonah (Yonah) in the Bible is literally named "dove". Noah's dove was a yona too.
Example (English): The dove is standing on the roof.

Mnemonic: bar-VAZ — a duck waddling into a BAR with a VASE. Silly enough to stick.
Example (English): The ducks swim in the lake.

Mnemonic: NEH-sher — a NASHER that snatches its prey. Israel's rescue helicopters and a whole town are named Nesher.
Example (English): The eagle flies high in the sky.

Mnemonic: yan-SHOOF — an owl going "shoof… shoof…" in the night. (Handily, shuf is Arabic slang for "look" — the owl is all eyes.)
Example (English): The owl is awake all night.

Mnemonic: chai-YAT mach-MAD — chaya = animal, machmad = darling/delight. A "darling animal".
Example (English): Do you have a pet at home?

Mnemonic: za-NAV — the tail NAVigates the animal. Also: a zanav is the "tail end" of a line.
Example (English): The dog has a long tail.

Mnemonic: RATS — rats run. Careful: ratz (runs) vs. rotze (wants) — one vowel apart.
Example (English): The boy runs very fast.

Mnemonic: KOH-fets — a jumping COFFEE POT rattling on the stove.
Example (English): The monkey jumps on the tree.

Mnemonic: SO-cheh — you swim so you don't SOAK and sink. Sounds a bit like "so-chill" — floating.
Example (English): I swim in the lake every morning.

Mnemonic: ROH-ked — dancing to ROCK music, in a CODE of steps. Hebrew hora dancing = rikud.
Example (English): They dance at the wedding all night.

Mnemonic: ZAZ — buzz-buzz, something that won't sit still. "Zuz!" is what Israelis shout for "Move it!"
Example (English): Don't move, I'm taking a picture!

Mnemonic: ROSH — Rosh Hashanah = "head of the year". Rosh is also a boss or a chief.
Example (English): My head hurts.

Mnemonic: seh-AR — think of a SHEAR, the tool for cutting hair. Usually used as a collective, no plural.
Example (English): She has long black hair.

Mnemonic: AH-yin — think of the "evil eye" charm, the ayin hara. Body parts that come in twos take the -ayim ending.
Example (English): He has green eyes.

Mnemonic: OH-zen — hamantaschen are called oznei Haman, "Haman's ears". Note the -ayim pair ending again.
Example (English): My ears hurt on the plane.

Mnemonic: AF — one syllable, like a sniff. Af also means "not even / none at all": af echad = nobody.
Example (English): My nose is blocked.

Mnemonic: ya-SHAN — the same root as yashen (asleep). Old things have been sleeping a long time. Use for objects, never people.
Example (English): The old car still runs.

Mnemonic: cha-DASH — the twin of chodesh (month): the new moon. Chadashot = the news, "the new things".
Example (English): I have a new phone.

Mnemonic: za-KEN — from zakan, "beard". The old man is the bearded one. Use for living things only.
Example (English): The old dog sleeps all day.

Mnemonic: tsa-EER — a young person is EAGER. (Careful: tza'if = scarf, one letter apart.)
Example (English): She's too young for this role.

Mnemonic: a-TEEK — an ANTIQUE. Same word, same root. Ha-Ir ha-Atika = the Old City of Jerusalem.
Example (English): We visited the Old City.

Mnemonic: PEH — the sound your mouth makes spitting something out: "peh!" Also the letter פ.
Example (English): Open your mouth, please.

Mnemonic: SHEN — you SHINE your teeth. A dentist is a rofe shinayim, a "teeth doctor".
Example (English): I brush my teeth twice a day.

Mnemonic: ga-BA — from gav (back): the eyebrow is the "back" or ridge above the eye.
Example (English): She raises an eyebrow in surprise.

Mnemonic: MO-ach — "MORE, ACH!" — the organ that always wants more. Slang: yesh lo moach = "he's smart".
Example (English): The human brain is complicated.

Mnemonic: OR — careful: or (עוֹר) = skin, but or (אוֹר) = light. Same sound, different first letter.
Example (English): I have skin that's sensitive to the sun.

Mnemonic: ro-EH — a ROE deer that you SEE in the field. Lehitraot ("see you") comes from this root.
Example (English): I see the sea from the window.

Mnemonic: sho-MEH-a — "Shma Yisrael" — HEAR, O Israel. Same root, ancient and everywhere.
Example (English): Do you hear the music?

Mnemonic: mak-SHEEV — to listen you have to make it "SHHH". Shomea = hear by accident; makshiv = listen on purpose.
Example (English): He doesn't listen to me at all.

Mnemonic: mis-ta-KEL — "Miss, take a look!" The mis-/mit- start marks a reflexive verb: you turn your own eyes.
Example (English): She's looking at the picture.

Mnemonic: meh-REE-ach — the smell REACHES your nose. Reach = riach.
Example (English): I smell fresh bread.

Mnemonic: YAD — the hamsa charm is also called a yad. The Torah pointer is a yad too — a little hand.
Example (English): Wash your hands before the meal.

Mnemonic: ETS-ba — "ETS-BAH!" — the sound of poking someone with a finger.
Example (English): I cut my finger in the kitchen.

Mnemonic: ka-TEF — you carry a bag on your shoulder, so it's the "CARRY-TEF". K-t-f is the root for carrying on the shoulder.
Example (English): My shoulder hurts from the backpack.

Mnemonic: GAV — think "GIVE me a back rub". Also the root of gaba (eyebrow) — a ridge.
Example (English): My back hurts from sitting.

Mnemonic: cha-ZEH — related to chazak (strong) in sound: a strong chest. Also the word for chicken breast on a menu.
Example (English): Chicken breast with vegetables, please.

Mnemonic: REH-gel — you get around on a REGULAR pair of legs. Ba-regel = "on foot"; kaduregel = soccer, "foot-ball".
Example (English): I walk to the store on foot.

Mnemonic: kaf = a scoop or palm. Your foot is literally "the scoop of the leg" — and kaf yad is the palm of your hand.
Example (English): The sand is hot on the soles of my feet.

Mnemonic: Hebrew has no separate word for "toe" — it's just a "finger of the leg". Nice and logical.
Example (English): I hurt my toe on the door.

Mnemonic: BEH-rech — the same root as bracha (blessing): you bend the knee to bless. Baruch = blessed.
Example (English): My knees hurt after the run.

Mnemonic: LEV — LOVE with a V. Sim lev = "pay attention" (literally "put heart").
Example (English): She has a good heart.

Mnemonic: me-da-BER — you talk and talk and it's a lot of DEBRIS/blah-blah. Dibur = speech.
Example (English): Do you speak Hebrew?

Mnemonic: oh-MER — "Oh, MORE?" is what you say. This is the everyday "say".
Example (Hebrew): מָה אַתְּ אוֹמֶרֶת? אֲנִי לֹא שׁוֹמֵעַ.
Example (translit): Ma at omeret? Ani lo shomea.
Example (English): What are you saying? I can't hear.

Mnemonic: ma-GID — a maggid was a wandering preacher who went town to town telling stories. Mostly used in the infinitive: Tagid li… = "Tell me…"
Example (English): Tell me the truth.

Mnemonic: me-sa-PER — same root as sefer (book) and sipur (story). A story-teller is a sofer/sapar of tales.
Example (English): Grandpa tells stories to the grandchildren.

Mnemonic: sho-EL — "Show 'ell, what's the answer?" She'ela = a question.
Example (English): The student asks a good question.

Mnemonic: sa-ME-ach — every Hebrew holiday greeting uses it: Chag sameach! Simcha = a joyous occasion.
Example (English): I'm happy to see you.

Mnemonic: mit-ra-GESH — from regesh (emotion), same as margish (feel). The mit- means it's happening inside you.
Example (English): I'm excited before the trip.

Mnemonic: geh-EH — sounds like a proud little "GAY-eh!" Ga'ava = pride; the Pride parade is Mitzad ha-Ga'ava.
Example (English): I'm proud of my sister.

Mnemonic: KEF — borrowed from Arabic kayf. "Eize kef!" = "How fun!" It's a noun really — "Yesh li kef" = I'm having fun.
Example (English): What fun at the sea today!

Mnemonic: me-an-YEN — from inyan, "a matter/interest". "Ein li inyan" = "I'm not interested".
Example (English): This lesson is very interesting.

Mnemonic: GOOF — your body is a big GOOFY machine. Guf also means "grammatical person" (first person = guf rishon).
Example (English): It's important to take care of your body.

Mnemonic: EH-tsem — etzem also means "an object" or "the essence of a thing": be-etzem = "actually, in essence".
Example (English): The dog eats a bone in the garden.

Mnemonic: KEH-va — think "CAVE-ah": the cave where your food goes.
Example (English): My stomach hurts after the meal.

Mnemonic: GEH-ver — a gever is a "man's man"; gvura = heroism. Isha = woman, from the same root as ish (man/person). Note the irregular plural nashim.
Example (Hebrew): יֵשׁ שְׁלוֹשָׁה גְּבָרִים וּשְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים בַּחֶדֶר.
Example (translit): Yesh shlosha gvarim ve-shtei nashim ba-cheder.
Example (English): There are three men and two women in the room.

Mnemonic: tee-NOK — a baby gives a little "TINY KNOCK" on the world.
Example (English): The baby girl is sleeping in the bed.

Mnemonic: ACH — "Ach sheli!" ("my brother!") is how Israeli men greet each other. Also the sound of a sigh.
Example (Hebrew): יֵשׁ לִי אָח אֶחָד וּשְׁתֵּי אֲחָיוֹת.
Example (translit): Yesh li ach echad ve-shtei achayot.
Example (English): I have one brother and two sisters.

Mnemonic: a-CHOT — brother + the feminine -ot. Achot also means "nurse" in a hospital.
Example (English): My sister lives in Haifa.

Mnemonic: BA-al — Baal was the Canaanite "lord". A ba'al is a master or owner — and, old-fashionedly, a husband.
Example (English): Her husband cooks excellently.

Mnemonic: shu-TAF — you SHARE the TAB. Shutafut = a partnership.
Example (English): My apartment roommate is very clean.

Mnemonic: GEES — "GEEZ, another in-law." Short and easy; add -a for the sister-in-law.
Example (English): My brother-in-law is coming to the meal.

Mnemonic: gee-SA — gis + the feminine -a. Hebrew is beautifully regular here.
Example (English): My sister-in-law is an architect.

Mnemonic: ka-LA — the same word covers "bride" and "daughter-in-law". Kala sounds like "call-ah" — the one being called into the family.
Example (English): The bride wears a white dress.

Mnemonic: cha-TAN — the groom at the chatuna (wedding). Same root: ch-t-n.
Example (English): The groom and bride are dancing.

Mnemonic: cho-REG — literally "deviating / outside the norm". Add it after the relative: ach choreg = stepbrother.
Example (English): My stepbrother lives in America.

Mnemonic: me-va-KESH — you request CASH. Bakasha = a request; bevakasha = "please / here you go".
Example (English): I'm asking for water, please.

Mnemonic: OH-neh — "Oh, NAY" is still an answer. Tshuva = an answer.
Example (English): She isn't answering the phone.

Mnemonic: mas-BEER — after a couple of BEERS everyone starts explaining everything.
Example (English): The teacher explains the lesson again.

Mnemonic: TSO-ek — sounds like a shriek itself: "tsoh-EK!" Half a shout, half a squawk.
Example (English): Don't shout, I'm not deaf!

Front (English): To be quiet / to shut up
Mnemonic: SHO-tek — "Shhh… take it down." Sheket! = "Quiet!" — same root.
Example (English): Everyone goes quiet when he speaks.

Mnemonic: ach-YAN — from ach (brother): your brother's kid. "Brother-ian".
Example (English): My nephew is five years old.

Mnemonic: ach-ya-NEET — nephew + the feminine -it ending.
Example (English): My niece studies ballet.

Mnemonic: NEH-ched — say "NEXT generation" — the neched is next in line.
Example (English): Grandma spoils her grandson.

Mnemonic: NECH-da — neched + the feminine -a.
Example (English): His granddaughter is three years old.

Mnemonic: NEEN — one generation further than neched, and one syllable shorter. Easy pair to remember together.
Example (English): He has three great-grandsons.

Mnemonic: nee-NA — nin + -a, exactly like neched/nechda.
Example (English): Her great-granddaughter was born yesterday.

Mnemonic: a-TSOOV — from etzev, sorrow. "A-TSOOB" — a sad, drooping sound.
Example (Hebrew): הוּא עָצוּב כִּי הֶחָבֵר שֶׁלּוֹ עָזַב.
Example (translit): Hu atzuv ki ha-chaver shelo azav.
Example (English): He's sad because his friend left.

Mnemonic: ko-ES — it even sounds like a cross "KO-ess!" Ka'as = anger.
Example (Hebrew): אַל תִּכְעַס עָלַי, זֶה הָיָה טָעוּת.
Example (translit): Al tich'as alai, ze haya ta'ut.
Example (English): Don't be angry at me, it was a mistake.

Mnemonic: ro-GEZ — a milder, sulkier version of ko'es. "Be-rogez" means two people aren't speaking to each other.
Example (English): They've been on bad terms since last week.

Mnemonic: di-ka-o-NEE — from dika'on, depression, from a root meaning "crushed down". Think "DECK-a-own" — pressed to the deck.
Example (English): The grey weather is depressing.

Mnemonic: me-tus-KAL — from tiskul, frustration. Say "me-too-SCOLD" — the feeling of being blocked at every turn.
Example (English): I'm frustrated with this job.

Mnemonic: o-RE-ach — from orach (a way/path): a guest is someone traveling your way. Hachnasat orchim = hospitality.
Example (English): The guests arrive at six.

Mnemonic: ZOOG — think "ZOO-G": animals boarded the ark two by two. Ben zug / bat zug = partner (male / female).
Example (English): I bought a new pair of socks.

Mnemonic: o-LEH — from la'alot, "to go up". Moving to Israel is aliyah — an ascent — so an immigrant is one who "goes up".
Example (English): The new immigrants study Hebrew at an ulpan.

Mnemonic: TEM-bel — a TUMBLE-brain. The classic Israeli sun hat is even called a kova tembel, an "idiot's hat".
Example (English): Don't be an idiot, take an umbrella.

Mnemonic: cha-YAL — from chayil, "strength/valor". Eshet chayil = "a woman of valor".
Example (English): The female soldier comes home for Shabbat.

Mnemonic: cho-SHEV — a machshev is a computer, the thinking machine. Same root: ch-sh-v.
Example (English): I think it's a good idea.

Mnemonic: yo-DEH-a — "Yo, DAY-a — do you know what day it is?" Use for facts and information.
Example (English): I don't know where the key is.

Front (English): To know (a person) / to be familiar with
Mnemonic: ma-KEER — "my DEAR" — the people you know dearly. Never use yodea for people.
Example (English): Do you know the new neighbor?

Mnemonic: meh-VEEN — "Me? BEEN there, so I understand."
Example (Hebrew): אֲנִי מְבִינָה אֶת הַמִּלָּה אֲבָל לֹא אֶת הַמִּשְׁפָּט.
Example (translit): Ani mevina et ha-mila aval lo et ha-mishpat.
Example (English): I understand the word but not the sentence.

Mnemonic: zo-CHER — "Yizkor" is the memorial prayer: remember. Think of a ZOO you'll never forget.
Example (English): Do you remember her name?

Mnemonic: ro-FEH — think of a doctor who says "ro-FEH, you'll be fine." Refua = medicine; refua shlema = "get well soon".
Example (English): The doctor examines the patient.

Other forms: pl. Rofei / Rofot shinayim רוֹפְאֵי / רוֹפְאוֹת שִׁנַּיִם
Mnemonic: Literally "teeth doctor" — Hebrew builds compound jobs by stacking nouns. Shen (tooth) → shinayim.
Example (Hebrew): אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ לְרוֹפֵא שִׁנַּיִם פַּעֲמַיִם בַּשָּׁנָה.
Example (translit): Ani holech le-rofe shinayim pa'amayim ba-shana.
Example (English): I go to the dentist twice a year.

Mnemonic: Straight from English — just add the -it for the feminine. Hebrew borrows freely for modern professions.
Example (English): She's a children's psychologist.

Mnemonic: me-ta-PEL — from letapel be-, "to take care of". A metapelet is also a nanny.
Example (English): The caregiver comes every morning.

Other forms: pl. Ovdim / Ovdot sotzialiyot עוֹבְדִים / עוֹבְדוֹת סוֹצְיָאלִיּוֹת
Mnemonic: oved = worker (from la'avod, to work) + sotzialit. Literally "social worker", word for word.
Example (English): The social worker helps the family.

Mnemonic: ma-TAI — "ma" starts most Hebrew question words: ma (what), matai (when), madua (why). Learn them as a family.
Example (English): When are you arriving?

Mnemonic: kshe- glues onto the front of the next word. Matai is only for questions; kshe- is for everything else. This trips up every learner — keep them apart.
Example (English): When he comes, we'll eat.

Mnemonic: kshe- + ani, written as one word. Same for ksheata, ksheat, kshehu, kshehi.
Example (Hebrew): כְּשֶׁאֲנִי עֲיֵפָה, אֲנִי לֹא מְדַבֶּרֶת טוֹב.
Example (translit): Ksheani ayefa, ani lo medaberet tov.
Example (English): When I'm tired, I don't speak well.

Front (English): When there is / when I have
Mnemonic: kshe- + yesh (there is). Yesh li = I have; so kshe-yesh li = "when I have".
Example (English): When I have time, I read.

Mnemonic: EI-zeh — also used for exclamations: "Eize yofi!" = "How lovely!" Eize for masculine, eizo for feminine.
Example (English): Which book are you reading?

Mnemonic: be- (in) + zman (time) + she- (that). Literally "in the time that". Hebrew builds connectors by stacking little pieces like this.
Example (English): While she cooks, I tidy up.

Other forms: pl. Orchei din / Orchot din עוֹרְכֵי דִּין / עוֹרְכוֹת דִּין
Mnemonic: orech = editor/arranger, din = law. A lawyer is literally "an arranger of the law".
Example (English): The lawyer reads the contract.

Mnemonic: sho-FET — the biblical Book of Judges is Shoftim. Also the referee in a soccer match.
Example (English): The judge makes a decision.

Mnemonic: sho-TER — a shoter will give you a TICKET. Mishtara = the police force.
Example (English): The police officer stops the car.

Mnemonic: ka-TSEEN — an officer is KEEN and in command. One rung above the chayal.
Example (English): The officer speaks with the soldiers.

Mnemonic: Exactly the verb lishmor turned into a person — Hebrew makes job titles this way constantly (kotev → writer, shomer → guard).
Example (English): The guard stands in front of the building.

Mnemonic: sho-KHE-ach — you forgot, so you SHRUG and say "ach!" The opposite twin of zocher.
Example (English): I always forget my glasses.

Mnemonic: ma-a-MEEN — say AMEN and you're a maamin. Literally the same root: a-m-n.
Example (English): I don't believe this story.

Mnemonic: me-ka-VEH — same root as Ha-Tikva, "the hope", Israel's anthem. Ani mekaveh = "hopefully", said constantly.
Example (English): I hope tomorrow will be warm.

Mnemonic: SHO-kel — the shekel was originally a WEIGHT. To consider is to weigh options — same word, same coin.
Example (English): We're considering moving to another city.

Mnemonic: me-cha-SHEV — one letter from choshev (thinks). Machshev = computer = the calculating machine.
Example (English): He's calculating how much it will cost.

Mnemonic: ad-ri-CHAL — a long, grand word for a person who designs grand things. Adrichalut = architecture.
Example (English): The architect draws the building.

Mnemonic: me-han-DES — think "my HANDS" — the person who builds with precision. Handasa = engineering (and geometry).
Example (English): The engineer works on a new bridge.

Mnemonic: chak-LAI — from chakla, an Aramaic word for field. Chakla'ut = agriculture, a proud Israeli word.

Mnemonic: ta-BACH — a chef who cooks up a BATCH. Mitbach (kitchen) is the same root: t-b-ch.

Mnemonic: MEL-tsar — the waiter is the little "TSAR" of your table, bringing the MEAL.

Mnemonic: cha-RED — literally "trembling". The ultra-Orthodox are called Charedim, "those who tremble before God".

Mnemonic: me-fu-CHAD — from pachad, fear. "Eize pachad!" = "How scary!"

Mnemonic: me-val-BEL — from bilbul, and back to the Tower of Babel. The word itself is a tongue-tangle.

Mnemonic: me-shu-GA — the Yiddish "meshugge" came straight from here. "Ata meshuga?!" is heard hourly in Israel.

Mnemonic: mu-ZAR — from zar, "a stranger/foreign". Something muzar is strange-ified.

Mnemonic: o-MAN — an artist is a craftsMAN. Omanut = art.

Mnemonic: tsa-YAR — from tzeva (color) and tziur (a drawing). A tzayar makes tziurim.

Mnemonic: so-FER — same root as sefer (book) and sipur (story). A sofer is also the scribe who writes a Torah scroll.

Mnemonic: ba-MAI — from bama, "a stage". The bamai is the one who runs the stage.

Mnemonic: LO-med — you're LOADING your brain, heading for MED school. Talmid (student) is the same root.

Mnemonic: me-la-MED — learn is lomed, teach is melamed: add the me- and you're causing someone else to learn.

Mnemonic: ko-REH — the Koran and the Mikra (Hebrew Bible) both mean "the reading/recitation". Kore also means "calls out".

Mnemonic: ko-TEV — think "quote-ev": writing down a quote. Michtav (letter) and ketovet (address) share the root.

Mnemonic: psan-TRAN — from psanter (piano) + the -an ending for a doer. Same pattern as kanar (violinist).

Mnemonic: ka-NAR — from kinor, the violin (and King David's harp was a kinor). "Fiddler on the Roof" is Kanar al ha-Gag.

Mnemonic: dug-MAN — from dugma, "an example". A model is literally a walking example.

Mnemonic: me-na-TSE-ach — nitzachon = victory. The orchestra conductor "conquers" the music — same word for both.

Mnemonic: na-HAG — from linhog, to drive. "Na-HAG" — he HUGS the wheel.

Mnemonic: mik-TSO-a — your profession is your "slice" of the world (from ketza, an edge/section). Also a school subject.

Mnemonic: hit-ma-CHOOT — from mumche, an expert. The hit- start means it's something you do to yourself: you make yourself an expert.

Mnemonic: TSEH-vet — a tight crew. Related to tzav, an order/command — a team under orders.

Mnemonic: mit-na-DEV — from nedava, a donation. The mit- prefix again: you give of yourself.

Mnemonic: maz-KEER — from lizkor (to remember): the secretary is the one who makes you remember. Same root: z-k-r.

Mnemonic: OH-chel — "Oh, KALE!" Ochel is also the noun "food".

Mnemonic: SHO-teh — a SHOT of something to drink.

Mnemonic: me-va-SHEL — cooking in a big SHELL/pot. Tavshil = a cooked dish.
Example (English): Dad is cooking vegetable soup.

Mnemonic: OH-feh — "Oh, fa-fa, it's hot!" An ofe is also the noun "baker".
Example (English): I'm baking a cake for a birthday.

Mnemonic: to-EM — you taste and say "mmm, TOO YUM." Ta'im = tasty.
Example (English): Taste the sauce, it's excellent.

Mnemonic: ra-EV — a hungry RAVEN. Ra'av = famine.
Example (English): I'm hungry, let's eat something.

Mnemonic: tsa-MEH — your throat is "tsa-MEH-parched". Learn it as the pair to ra'ev; they rhyme in structure.
Example (English): The children are thirsty after the game.

Mnemonic: a-YEF — a tired sigh: "ai-YEF…" Remember: with no verb "to be", "I'm tired" is just Ani ayef.

Mnemonic: CHO-leh — beit cholim, "house of the sick", is a hospital. A choleh is also "a patient".

Example (English): The girl is sick, she didn't go to school.

Mnemonic: ba-REE — "Be well!" is Titbari! Bri'ut = health, and it's what you say when someone sneezes.

Mnemonic: BEH-ged — you wear a BAGGED item. Usually used in the plural: begadim = clothes.

Mnemonic: chul-TSA — sounds like "HOLD-za" — the thing that holds your torso.
Example (English): The white shirt is dirty.

Mnemonic: mich-na-SA-yim — from lehachnis, "to put in": pants are what you put your legs INTO. Always dual, like all leg-and-eye words.

Mnemonic: sim-LA — a dress makes you SMILE-ah. Handy near sameach (happy).
Example (English): She's buying a dress for the wedding.

Mnemonic: cha-tsa-EET — from chetzi, "half": a skirt is half a dress. Perfectly logical.

Mnemonic: meh-EEL — a coat SEALS you in against the cold. "Me-SEAL."
Example (English): Take a coat, it's cold outside.

Mnemonic: cha-lee-FA — from lehachlif, "to change/swap": a suit is your change of clothes for special occasions.
Example (English): He wears a black suit to work.

Mnemonic: a-nee-VA — from la'anov, to knot. A tie is "the knotted thing".
Example (English): His tie is too colorful.

Mnemonic: cha-go-RA — a belt HUGS you around. Chagorat betichut = a seatbelt.
Example (English): Fasten your seatbelt in the car.

Mnemonic: KEES — you KEEP things in it. Kis also means a bag or a pouch.
Example (English): The key is in the pants pocket.

Mnemonic: NA-al — same root as lin'ol, the verb for wearing shoes. Dual ending because shoes come in twos.

Mnemonic: ma-GAF — a boot with a big GAFF/cuff at the top.
Example (English): In winter I wear boots.

Mnemonic: GEH-rev — sounds like "GRAB" — grab a pair of socks.

Mnemonic: Literally "house shoes" — na'alayim + bayit. Hebrew loves these transparent compounds.
Example (English): I wear slippers in the evening.

Mnemonic: kfa-FA — from kaf, the palm of the hand. A glove is "the palm-thing".
Example (English): You need gloves when it's very cold.

Front (English): To get up / to stand up
Mnemonic: KAM — "Come on, get up!" Kum! is what a parent shouts in the morning.
Example (English): I get up at six in the morning.

Mnemonic: yo-SHEV — same root as Shabbat, the day you sit and rest. Also moshav, a place people sit/settle.
Example (English): We sit in the living room and talk.

Mnemonic: oh-MED — standing like a column: amud means "pillar" (and "page").
Example (English): They're standing in line for the register.

Mnemonic: NACH — Noah (Noach) rested after the flood. Menucha = rest.
Example (English): I rest after work.

Mnemonic: nish-AR — what's left over is the SHARE that stays behind.
Example (English): I'm staying home this evening.

Mnemonic: KO-va — a hat COVERS you. Ko-va / co-ver: close enough to stick.
Example (English): Put on a hat, the sun is strong.

Mnemonic: tsa-EEF — it wraps you and you feel SAFE. (Careful: tza'ir = young, one letter apart.)
Example (English): The red scarf matches the coat.

Mnemonic: mish-ka-FA-yim — from lehashkif, "to look out". Two lenses, so the -ayim dual ending.

Example (translit): Ani lo ro'eh klum bli mishkafayim.
Example (English): I can't see anything without glasses.

Mnemonic: Glasses + shemesh (sun). Compound again: "glasses of sun".
Example (English): I forgot my sunglasses in the car.

Mnemonic: yal-KOOT — a YELLOW KIT on your back. Every Israeli schoolkid carries one.
Example (English): The child's backpack is very heavy.

Mnemonic: CHAM — chamsin is the hot desert wind. Chamin is the slow-cooked Shabbat stew — the hot dish.
Example (English): The coffee is too hot to drink.

Mnemonic: KAR — a cold CAR in the morning. Kor = the cold; mekarer = fridge, the cold-maker.
Example (English): It's cold outside, take a coat.

Mnemonic: ra-TOOV — from the same family as rotev, sauce (the wet stuff). Both from r-t-v.
Example (English): The clothes are still wet.

Mnemonic: ya-VESH — the dry land God separated from the sea is yabasha. Say "ya-VESH" like something crackling dry.
Example (English): The bread is dry from yesterday.

Mnemonic: MAR — the bitter herbs at Passover are maror. Mar is also the polite title "Mr." — different word, same sound.
Example (English): This coffee is very bitter.

Mnemonic: tach-SHEET — a fancy sheet of metal. Slang bonus: calling a kid a tachshit means "you little piece of work".
Example (English): She buys jewelry at the market.

Mnemonic: ta-BA-at — from tova (to sink/stamp) — a signet ring stamps a seal. The Lord of the Rings is Sar Ha-Taba'ot.
Example (English): Her ring is made of gold.

Mnemonic: tsa-MEED — from tzamud, "attached/stuck to". A bracelet stays attached to your wrist.

Mnemonic: shar-SHEH-ret — say it fast and it rattles like links: shar-sheh-ret.
Example (English): This necklace is ancient.

Mnemonic: sha-ON — from sha'a (hour). A watch is "the hour-thing".
Example (English): My watch is five minutes slow.

Mnemonic: tach-PO-set — from lechapes (to search) — a costume makes people search for who you really are. Purim is the tachposet holiday.

Mnemonic: lo-KE-ach — "LOW, CATCH it!" — reach down and take.
Example (English): I'm taking my backpack.

Mnemonic: no-TEN — "No? TEN, then" — handing over ten shekels. Matana (gift) is the same root: n-t-n.

Mnemonic: meh-VEE — "Me? V.I.P. — I bring the goods." Related to la-vo (to come): bringing = causing to come.

Mnemonic: SAM — "Sam, put it down." Sim lev = "put heart" = pay attention.
Example (English): Put the book on the table.

Mnemonic: mach-ZEEK — you hold on because your grip is chazak (strong). Same root: ch-z-k.
Example (English): She's holding the baby in her arms.

Mnemonic: dee-RA — you get a DEAL on a DIRA. Most Israelis live in one, so you'll hear it constantly.

Mnemonic: CHEH-der — the Jewish one-room schoolhouse was called a cheder. Note the vowel flip in the plural: cheder → chadarim.

Mnemonic: GAG — two letters, shaped like a little roof: ג is even pointy on top.

Mnemonic: GAN — Gan Eden = the Garden of Eden. A kindergarten is a gan yeladim, "children's garden".

Mnemonic: sa-LON — straight from the French "salon". A freebie.

Mnemonic: SHO-ver — a SHOVE breaks it. Shavur = broken.

Mnemonic: me-ta-KEN — "Me? TAKE 'N fix it." Tikkun olam = repairing the world.

Mnemonic: DEH-let — the door LETS you in: de-LET. Also the Hebrew letter ד, dalet.

Mnemonic: cha-LON — you stare out the window for a LONG time.

Mnemonic: a-RON — the Ark of the Covenant is the Aron ha-Brit, and the Torah cabinet in a synagogue is the aron kodesh. It's a big box.

Mnemonic: vee-LON — a VEIL that's LONG. Borrowed from the same European root as "voile".

Mnemonic: mee-TA — a bed is roughly a METER wide. (Don't confuse with mata = downward.)
Example (English): The cat sleeps on my bed.

Mnemonic: me-ka-RER — from kar (cold). The mekarer is "the cold-maker".

Mnemonic: cha-SHOOV — from lachshov (to think): important things are the ones worth thinking about.

Mnemonic: ma-GEH-vet — from lenagev, "to wipe dry". Again the ma- tool-prefix: the drying-tool.

Mnemonic: niyar = paper (think "NEAR" — always keep it near). Then the borrowed "toalet".

Mnemonic: ZEH-vel — originally "manure". Israelis use it for garbage and, in slang, for anything terrible: "Ha-seret haya zevel."

Mnemonic: TO-fes — you catch it and it's TOO FAST. Also means "to grab a seat/spot".

Mnemonic: ke-a-RA — a bowl is CURVED — "ke-CURVE-ah".

Mnemonic: a-GAS — a pear shaped like a little GAS balloon.

Mnemonic: REE-ba — a RIBBON of jam across your toast.
Example (English): I spread jam on the bread.

Mnemonic: mar-GEESH — a feeling is a RUSH, spelled backwards-ish. Regesh = an emotion.
Example (English): I feel better today.

Mnemonic: me-fa-NEK — you PAMPER by nuzzling someone's NECK. Mefunak = spoiled (in a cute way).
Example (English): Grandma spoils the grandchildren.

Mnemonic: so-LE-ach — Slicha! ("sorry / excuse me") is the word you'll say twenty times a day. Same root: s-l-ch.
Example (English): I forgive you, it's fine.

Mnemonic: me-a-CHEL — "May I A-KHEL you well." Note: this is wishing someone something, not wanting (that's rotze).
Example (English): I wish you success!

Mnemonic: mas-KEEM — agreeing to the SCHEME. Haskama = agreement/consent.
Example (English): I agree with you completely.

Mnemonic: ba-KAR — cattle you'd haul in a big CAR. Basar bakar = beef.
Example (English): I don't eat beef.

Mnemonic: OF — from la'uf, "to fly": poultry is "the flying thing". Different word from the live bird (tarnegol).
Example (English): The chicken has been in the oven for an hour.

Mnemonic: cha-ZEER — sounds like a snorting "cha-ZEEEER". Slang: calling someone a chazir means they're a slob.
Example (English): They don't eat pork.

Mnemonic: chem-A — from cham (warm)? No — but it helps: butter melts when it's cham. Chem'at botnim = peanut butter.
Example (English): Put butter on the warm bread.

Mnemonic: KEH-mach — "Im ein kemach, ein Torah" — "without flour there's no Torah", an old saying about needing bread before books.
Example (English): We need flour for the cake.

Mnemonic: ZOL — cheap enough that you SOLD it fast. "Ze zol!" is a bargain shopper's cry at the shuk.
Example (English): The vegetables are cheap at the market.

Mnemonic: ya-KAR — like English "dear", it means both costly and beloved. A letter starts "Yakar sheli" — "my dear".
Example (English): This apartment is too expensive.

Mnemonic: ma-LEH — also what you say after a big meal: "Ani maleh!" Milui = a filling.
Example (English): The bus is full of people.

Mnemonic: REK — an empty WRECK. Learn it paired with maleh.
Example (English): The fridge is completely empty.

Mnemonic: ka-VED — kaved is also the liver, the body's heaviest organ. And kavod (honor) is the same root: honor has weight.
Example (English): The suitcase is too heavy for me.

Mnemonic: a-ROO-cha — arucha sounds like "a ROUTINE" — the routine three a day. Arucḥat boker = breakfast.
Example (English): Dinner is at eight.

Mnemonic: kee-NOO-ach — from lekanach, "to wipe clean": dessert is what wipes the meal clean at the end.
Example (English): What's for dessert?

Mnemonic: mam-TEEK — from matok (sweet). The ma- prefix means "the thing that makes it so": the sweetener.
Example (English): I don't put sweetener in my coffee.

Mnemonic: RO-tev — from ratuv, "wet". Sauce is the wet stuff.
Example (English): The sauce is too spicy for me.

Mnemonic: cha-tee-CHA — from lachtoch, "to cut": a piece is a cut-off bit. Slang warning: calling a person a chatich(a) means "hottie".
Example (English): I want another piece of cake.

Mnemonic: nif-GASH — two people meet and GASH into each other. Pgisha = a meeting.
Example (English): We're meeting at a café at four.

Mnemonic: me-va-KER — you drive your CAR to visit. Bikur = a visit; careful, mevaker also means "criticizes".
Example (English): I'm visiting the family in Haifa.

Mnemonic: oh-ZER — "Oh, ZORRO to the rescue!" Ezra = help; ozeret also means "housekeeper".
Example (English): Can you help me please?

Mnemonic: TO-mech — a support beam holds up the TOMB. Tmicha = support.
Example (English): The parents support her decision.

Mnemonic: SHO-mer — a shomer stands at every Israeli mall entrance. "Show, MORE security."
Example (English): The guard watches over the entrance.

Mnemonic: mash-KEH — from lehashkot, "to give drink". Related to the mashkeh (cupbearer) in the Joseph story.
Example (Hebrew): מָה אַתָּה רוֹצֶה לִשְׁתּוֹת? יֵשׁ מַשְׁקָאוֹת קָרִים.
Example (translit): Ma ata rotze lishtot? Yesh mashkaot karim.
Example (English): What do you want to drink? There are cold drinks.

Mnemonic: charif means "sharp/spicy" — so alcohol is literally "a sharp drink". Same word you'd use for spicy food.
Example (English): He doesn't drink alcoholic beverages.

Mnemonic: MEETS — juice that MEETS your thirst. Short and easy.
Example (English): Fresh orange juice, please.

Mnemonic: taf-REET — from prat, "a detail": a menu is the itemized list of details.
Example (English): The waiter gives us a menu.

Mnemonic: mat-KON — from tochen, "content": a recipe is the "contents plan". Sounds like "MAT-CON" — matching the contents.
Example (English): This is my grandmother's recipe.

Mnemonic: mits-RACH — from tzarich, "needed": an ingredient is literally "a needed thing". Mitzrachim = groceries.
Example (English): I bought all the ingredients for the recipe.

Mnemonic: lif-NEI — from panim, "face": before = in front of the face of. Works for time and place both.
Example (English): I brush my teeth before sleep.

Mnemonic: a-cha-REI — same family as acharon (last) and me'uchar (late). The pair to lifnei.
Example (English): We'll talk after the meal.

Mnemonic: BEIN — "BETWEEN" even starts the same way. Bein…le-bein… = "between X and Y". It takes personal endings: beini u-veincha = "between me and you".
Example (English): What's the difference between the two?

Mnemonic: mi-TA-chat — from tachat, "under". Always followed by le-: mitachat la-shulchan.
Example (English): The cat is under the bed.

Mnemonic: MOOL — you stand "MULL-ing" it over, face to face. Mul ha-bayit = across from the house.
Example (English): The store is opposite the station.

Mnemonic: ma-KOM — from lakum (to rise/stand): a place is where something stands. Ha-Makom ("The Place") is even a name for God.
Example (English): This is a nice place for a meal.

Mnemonic: EER — you HEAR the city. Iriya = the city hall. Note the vowel change in the plural: ir → arim.
Example (English): Tel Aviv is a big and noisy city.

Mnemonic: EH-rets — Eretz Yisrael. Artzot ha-Brit ("lands of the covenant") = the United States.
Example (English): Which country do you live in?

Mnemonic: kto-VET — from lichtov (to write): an address is "the written thing". Also means a tattoo or an inscription.
Example (English): What's the office's address?

Mnemonic: DEH-rech — "derech eretz" means good manners, literally "the way of the land". Also used for "via / by way of".
Example (English): The road to the sea is long.

Mnemonic: oh-VED — an OVERWORKED employee. Avoda = work; the root a-v-d also gave us "slave" (eved).
Example (English): She works in a big office.

Mnemonic: me-sha-LEM — paying makes things SHALEM (whole/complete) — same root as shalom. You settle the debt.
Example (English): I'm paying by credit card.

Mnemonic: KO-neh — you buy an ice cream CONE, eh? Kniya = a purchase; kniyot = shopping.
Example (English): We buy vegetables at the market.

Mnemonic: me-ka-BEL — the Kabbalah is "the received tradition". Kabbala is also the receipt you get at a shop.
Example (translit): Kibalti matana yafa. / Ani mekabel michtav.
Example (English): I'm receiving a letter.

Mnemonic: BO-cher — you choose a BACHELOR from the lineup. Bechira = choice/election.
Example (English): It's hard for me to choose from the menu.

Mnemonic: cha-NOOT — a shop where you HAND OUT goods. Sounds like "HA-noot".
Example (English): The store is closed on Saturday.

Mnemonic: mis-RAD — the mi- place-prefix again + sherut (service). A misrad is also a government ministry.
Example (Hebrew): אֲנִי עוֹבֵד בַּמִּשְׂרָד מִתֵּשַׁע עַד חָמֵשׁ.
Example (translit): Ani oved ba-misrad me-tesha ad chamesh.
Example (English): I work in the office from nine to five.

Mnemonic: Literally "house of book". Bayit becomes beit when glued to another noun — beit cholim (hospital, "house of the sick"), beit kafe (café).
Example (English): The children go to school in the morning.

Mnemonic: sif-ree-YA — from sefer (book) + the -iya ending Hebrew uses for shops and places: sifriya, pitzeriya, mispara (barber).
Example (English): I'm returning books to the library.

Mnemonic: ma-LON — from lalun, "to stay the night". Careful: malon = hotel, melon = the fruit.
Example (English): I booked a room at the hotel for three nights.

Mnemonic: ma-HEER — maher is the adverb, "quickly": "Bo maher!" = "Come quickly!"
Example (English): The train is faster than the bus.

Mnemonic: ee-TEE — the adverb is le'at, "slowly": "Le'at, le'at" = "Slowly, slowly" — a very Israeli piece of advice.
Example (English): The internet here is very slow.

Mnemonic: ka-ROV — a krov mishpacha is a relative — someone "close". Also from lekarev, to bring near.
Example (English): The store is close to the house.

Mnemonic: ra-CHOK — sounds like a long throw: "ra-CHOOOK". The opposite of karov.
Example (English): The airport is far from here.

Mnemonic: ya-SHAR — Yisrael means "one who wrestles with God", but yashar on its own means straight and upright. Directions: "Tamshich yashar!"
Example (English): Continue straight and then left.

Mnemonic: namal = a port, te'ufa = flying. An airport is literally "a port of flight".
Example (English): We arrive at the airport at four.

Mnemonic: ta-cha-NA — from lachanot, "to encamp": a station is where you camp for a moment. Tachana merkazit = central bus station.
Example (English): The next stop is mine.

Mnemonic: dar-KON — from derech (road/way): a passport is your "road document".
Example (English): Don't forget your passport at home!

Mnemonic: tee-YOOL — Israelis are obsessed with the tiyul. It covers everything from a stroll to a six-month backpacking trek.
Example (English): We're taking a trip in the north.

Mnemonic: tnu-A — from lanua, "to move". Also means a political or youth movement, and a Hebrew vowel.
Example (English): There's a lot of traffic in the morning.

Mnemonic: SO-cher — you're the one who SEARCHES for a place. S-ch-r = wages/hire. This is the tenant's verb.
Example (English): We're renting an apartment in Tel Aviv.

Mnemonic: mas-KEER — the ma-/me- prefix makes it causative: you CAUSE someone to rent. This is the landlord's verb.
Example (English): He rents out the apartment to students.

Mnemonic: mach-ZEER — chozer = you go back; machzir = you SEND something back. Same pattern as socher/maskir.
Example (English): I'm returning the book to the library.

Mnemonic: Same verb as "to guard" — in Hebrew, keeping and guarding are one idea. Lishmor al = to take care of.
Example (English): I keep the receipts.

Mnemonic: GO-nev — a GONIF is Yiddish for a thief, straight from this Hebrew root. "Lo tignov" = Thou shalt not steal.
Example (English): Someone stole my bicycle.

Mnemonic: knee-SA — from lehikanes, "to enter". You'll see כניסה on every doorway in Israel.
Example (English): Entrance to the museum is free.

Mnemonic: yetz-ee-A — from latzet (to go out). Yetziat Mitzrayim = the Exodus from Egypt. Learn it as the pair to knisa.
Example (English): Where's the nearest exit?

Mnemonic: a-GAM — a lake you'd want to go swimming in AGAIN.
Example (English): The lake is quiet in the morning.

Mnemonic: ma-sa-EET — from masa, "a load". A truck is "the load-carrier".
Example (English): The truck is blocking the road.

Mnemonic: she-ROOT — from lesharet, to serve. Useful trap: in the plural, sherutim means "the toilets". A sherut is also a shared taxi.
Example (English): Where's the bathroom, please?

Mnemonic: sof = end, shavua = week. "End of week" — and in Israel that's Friday–Saturday, not Saturday–Sunday.
Example (English): What are you doing this weekend?

Mnemonic: SEH-fer — the Sefer Torah. Also sofer (writer), sifriya (library), sipur (story) — one big family.
Example (English): This book is very interesting.

Mnemonic: see-POOR — from lesaper (to tell). "Ze sipur acher" = "that's another story."
Example (English): Grandpa tells a story before bed.

Mnemonic: mee-LA — a MILLION words to learn. (Mila also means circumcision — brit mila — from a different root.)
Example (Hebrew): אֲנִי לוֹמֶדֶת חָמֵשׁ מִלִּים חֲדָשׁוֹת כָּל יוֹם.
Example (translit): Ani lomedet chamesh milim chadashot kol yom.
Example (English): I learn five new words every day.

Mnemonic: a-MOOD — from la'amod (to stand): a pillar stands, and a page "stands" in a book. Same word for both.
Example (English): Open the book to page twenty.

Mnemonic: shee-OOR — a shiur is a Torah class, and also a school lesson. Shiurei bayit = homework.
Example (English): I have a Hebrew lesson at four.

Mnemonic: mat-CHEEL — you start and then you CHILL. Hatchala = a beginning.
Example (English): The movie starts at eight.

Mnemonic: mam-SHEECH — you keep going and it's a long SCHLEP. Hemshech = a sequel/continuation.
Example (English): Keep walking straight ahead.

Mnemonic: GO-mer — "GO, MORE? No — I'm done." Gamarnu! = "We're finished!"
Example (English): I finish work at five.

Mnemonic: oh-TSER — the red octagon says עֲצוֹר (atzor) on every Israeli road. Think "OH! STOP-zer."
Example (English): The bus stops at the next station.

Mnemonic: me-sha-NEH — shana = year, and every year things change. Lo meshane = "it doesn't matter / never mind".
Example (Hebrew): הוּא מְשַׁנֶּה אֶת הַתָּכְנִית כָּל יוֹם.
Example (translit): Hu meshane et ha-tochnit kol yom.
Example (English): He changes the plan every day.

Mnemonic: muk-DAM — from kodem, "before/prior". Also used as an adverb: "Kamti mukdam" = "I got up early".
Example (English): I arrived early to the meeting.

Mnemonic: me-u-CHAR — from achar, "after". Related to acharei (after) and acharon (last) — a whole family.
Example (English): It's already late, I'm going home.

Mnemonic: ree-SHON — from rosh (head): first is at the head. Yom rishon = Sunday, the "first day".
Example (English): This is my first time here.

Mnemonic: a-cha-RON — from achar, after. The last one comes after everyone. Pairs with rishon.
Example (English): This is the last bus of the night.

Mnemonic: mu-CHAN — from lehachin, to prepare. "At muchana?" = "Are you ready?" — you'll hear it constantly.
Example (English): The meal is ready, come eat.

Mnemonic: ET — two letters, like a pen stroke. Careful with the sound-alike et (אֶת), the object marker you use in every sentence.
Example (Hebrew): יֵשׁ לְךָ עֵט? אֲנִי רוֹצָה לִכְתֹּב מַשֶּׁהוּ.
Example (translit): Yesh lecha et? Ani rotza lichtov mashehu.
Example (English): Do you have a pen? I want to write something.

Mnemonic: ee-pa-RON — from afar, "dust/graphite". A pencil is the dusty writer.
Example (English): The pencil is broken, it needs sharpening.

Mnemonic: mach-BEH-ret — from lechaber, "to join/compose": a notebook is bound pages joined together. Chaver (friend) is the same root — one who is joined to you.
Example (English): I write the words in the notebook.

Mnemonic: GEER — chalk that makes you go "GRR" when it squeaks.
Example (English): The teacher writes with chalk on the board.

Mnemonic: KAV — two letters, straight like a line. Also a bus route: kav 5 = the number 5 line.
Example (English): Draw a straight line in the notebook.

Mnemonic: mich-TAV — from lichtov (to write). Note: this is a letter you MAIL. A letter of the alphabet is an ot.
Example (English): I got a letter from the bank.

Mnemonic: ee-TON — from et, "time": a newspaper is "the time-thing", like the English "Times".
Example (English): Dad reads a newspaper every morning.

Mnemonic: cha-da-SHOT — literally "new things", the plural of chadash (new). Only ever used in the plural.
Example (English): The news starts at eight.

Mnemonic: mis-PAR — from lispor, "to count". Sounds like "miss PAR" — off by a number.
Example (English): What's your phone number?

Mnemonic: tshoo-VA — from lashuv, "to return": an answer is what comes back. Also "repentance" — a return to the right path.
Example (English): I don't have an answer to this question.

Mnemonic: tmoo-NA — think of a picture you MOUNT on the wall: t-MOUNT-a.
Example (English): There are beautiful pictures on the wall.

Mnemonic: tsee-YOOR — from letzayer, to draw, and tzayar, a painter. A tziur is what a tzayar makes.
Example (English): The girl's drawing is colorful.

Mnemonic: DOOG-ma — same root as dugman, a model. Lemashal / le-dugma = "for example".
Example (English): Give me an example, please.

Mnemonic: may-DA — from lada'at, "to know": information is "knowable stuff". You'll see מידע on every info desk.
Example (Hebrew): אֵין לִי מַסְפִּיק מֵידָע עַל הַטִּיּוּל.
Example (translit): Ein li mespik meida al ha-tiyul.
Example (English): I don't have enough information about the trip.

Mnemonic: cho-VEH-ret — from lechaber (to join), just like machberet. A choveret is a thin stapled booklet.
Example (English): I got a booklet with all the details.

Mnemonic: Booklet + avoda (work). Hebrew stacks nouns to build compounds — you've now seen this a dozen times.
Example (English): The students open the workbook.

Mnemonic: HO-fech — to flip something over. Hafuch is the Israeli latte — literally "upside down" coffee.
Example (English): The water turns into ice.

Mnemonic: ga-DEL — one letter from gadol (big). To grow is to become gadol.
Example (English): The children grow so fast.

Mnemonic: po-RE-ach — perach means flower; to bloom is to "do a flower". Same root: p-r-ch.
Example (English): The flowers bloom in spring.

Mnemonic: BO-neh — the BONES of a house. Binyan = a building (and also the name for a Hebrew verb pattern).
Example (English): They're building a new house in the neighborhood.

Mnemonic: yo-TSER — the Yotzer is the Creator in Hebrew liturgy. Yetzira = a creation/artwork.
Example (English): The artist creates new music.

Mnemonic: sha-A — related to shaon (watch/clock). Ma ha-sha'a? = "What time is it?"
Example (English): I waited a whole hour.

Mnemonic: da-KA — from dak, "thin/fine": a minute is a fine slice of an hour. "Rega, daka!" = "Wait, one minute!"
Example (English): I'll arrive in ten minutes.

Mnemonic: shnee-YA — from shtayim/sheni, "two/second". Just like English: the "second" division of an hour.
Example (English): Just a second, I'm coming!

Mnemonic: sha-NA — Rosh Hashana = "head of the year". Shana tova = happy new year.
Example (English): I've lived here for three years.

Mnemonic: CHO-desh — from chadash, "new": a month begins with the new moon. Watch the near-twins: chodesh (month) vs. chadash (new).
Example (English): Next month we're traveling abroad.

Mnemonic: pa-NOO-ee — from lefanot, "to clear out". A free table, a free evening, or a single person are all panui.
Example (English): Are you free tomorrow evening?

Mnemonic: a-SOOK — from esek, "business". A busy person is deep in their esek.
Example (English): I'm busy all week.

Mnemonic: sha-KET — "Sheket!" is what a teacher shouts for silence. Same root as shotek (to be quiet).
Example (English): The neighborhood is quiet at night.

Mnemonic: ra-a-SHAN — from ra'ash, noise. A ra'ashan is also the noisemaker you spin at Purim.
Example (English): The restaurant is too noisy.

Mnemonic: me-cha-KEH — from lechakot, to wait. "Ani mechakeh le…" is how you say you're looking forward to something.
Example (English): I'm looking forward to the weekend.

Mnemonic: hat-cha-LA — from lehatchil (to begin). Bereshit, the first word of the Torah, means "in the beginning" — but hatchala is the everyday word.
Example (English): This is only the beginning.

Mnemonic: a-VAR — from la'avor, "to pass": the past is what has passed. It's also the name of the past tense — your Phase 2 material.
Example (English): In the past I lived in Jerusalem.

Mnemonic: haf-sa-KA — from lehafsik, "to stop". School recess, a coffee break, and a theatre intermission are all a hafsaka.
Example (Hebrew): בּוֹאִי נִקַּח הַפְסָקָה שֶׁל עֶשֶׂר דַּקּוֹת.
Example (translit): Bo'i nikach hafsaka shel eser dakot.
Example (English): Let's take a ten-minute break.

Mnemonic: LOO-ach — the Ten Commandments were on luchot ha-brit, stone tablets. A luach shana is a yearly calendar, and a classroom blackboard is a luach too.
Example (English): The calendar hangs on the kitchen wall.

Mnemonic: me-cha-PES — searching until you're out of PEP. Chipus = a search.
Example (English): I'm looking for my glasses.

Mnemonic: mo-TSEH — "MAZEL! I found it." Metzia = a bargain, literally "a find".
Example (Hebrew): אֲנִי לֹא מוֹצֵאת אֶת הַכְּתֹבֶת בַּמַּפָּה.
Example (English): I can't find the address on the map.

Mnemonic: me-ga-LEH — to un-cover, like a GALLERY revealing a painting. Gilui = a discovery.
Example (translit): Giliti sod. / Ani megale ma kara.
Example (English): I'm finding out what happened.

Mnemonic: BO-dek — a doctor checks you on the DECK. Bdika = a test/checkup.
Example (English): The doctor examines the patients.

Mnemonic: KO-lel — from kol (all): to include is to take in ALL of it. Ha-mechir kolel… = "the price includes…"
Example (English): The price includes a meal and a drink.

Mnemonic: ra-a-YON — an idea that goes ON and ON. "Yesh li ra'ayon!" = "I have an idea!"
Example (English): I have an excellent idea.

Mnemonic: SEE-ba — a reason you can SEE. Mi-siba she… = "for the reason that…"
Example (English): There's no reason to worry.

Mnemonic: eh-MET — say AMEN and you affirm the emet. Same root a-m-n as "believe".
Example (English): Tell me the truth, please.

Mnemonic: ta-OOT — you went off route: "ta-OUT of the way". "Ta'ut be-mispar" = "wrong number" on the phone.
Example (English): I made a mistake in the calculation.

Mnemonic: hev-DEL — from lehavdil, "to separate". Havdala is the Saturday-night ceremony separating Shabbat from the week.
Example (English): What's the difference between the two?

Mnemonic: RAK — "RACK up only one." Tiny word, enormous usage: "Rak rega!" = "Just a moment!"
Example (English): I only have five minutes.

Mnemonic: chutz = outside, mi- = from. "Outside of" — everything except that. Note how it pairs with bachutz below.
Example (English): Everyone came except Dani.

Mnemonic: a-fee-LOO — "a FEE, TOO?! Even that?" Afilu lo = "not even".
Example (English): He works even on Saturday.

Mnemonic: ha-CHEE makes superlatives: hachi tov = the best, hachi gadol = the biggest. Rov means "the majority of": rov ha-anashim = most people.
Example (English): This is the most beautiful place in the city.

Mnemonic: ba-CHOOTS — be- (in) + chutz (outside). Chul (חו"ל) is the abbreviation for "abroad", literally "outside the land".
Example (English): It's cold outside, close the door.

Mnemonic: bil-BOOL — from the Tower of BABEL (Bavel), where all the languages got confused. The word even sounds jumbled.
Example (English): There was a big mix-up at the station.

Mnemonic: TSEH-va — from litzbo'a (to paint). Eize tzeva ata ohev? = "What color do you like?"
Example (English): What color is her dress?

Mnemonic: DEH-gel — a flag with a DANGLE. Degel Yisrael = the Israeli flag.
Example (English): The flag waves in the wind.

Mnemonic: ma-ta-NA — from latet (to give), root n-t-n. A gift is "a given thing".
Example (English): I got a lovely gift from my sister.

Mnemonic: o-TSAR — an OZ-like hoard. Sar ha-otzar = the finance minister, "minister of the treasury".
Example (English): The children are looking for treasure in the sand.

Mnemonic: me-ga-NEN — a gan is a garden (and a kindergarten — a "children's garden"). Ganan = gardener.
Example (English): Grandpa gardens in the garden every Saturday.

Mnemonic: tso-VEH-a — tzeva = color. To paint is to "do color" onto something.
Example (English): We're painting the wall white.

Mnemonic: Same word as paint — Hebrew doesn't split "paint" and "color". Context does the work.
Example (English): The girl colors in the drawing.

Mnemonic: me-sa-CHEK — you play and you CHECK the score. Mischak = a game; sachkan = a player/actor.
Example (English): The children play soccer in the park.

Mnemonic: SHAR — shir means "song", so lashir = "to song". Shir Ha-Shirim = Song of Songs.
Example (English): She sings in a choir.

Mnemonic: PEH-rach — from lifro'ach, "to bloom". Perach also means a cadet or trainee — someone still blooming.
Example (English): I bought flowers for the table.

Mnemonic: a-LEH — from la'alot, "to go up": a leaf grows upward. Same word family as oleh (immigrant) and aliyah.
Example (English): The leaves are red in autumn.

Mnemonic: GAL — a wave that gives you a GALLON of water. Galgal (wheel) is gal doubled — something that rolls.
Example (English): The waves are high at the sea today.

Mnemonic: ma-BOOL — Noah's Flood is Ha-Mabul. Israelis use it for any downpour: "Yesh mabul ba-chutz!"
Example (Hebrew): יֵשׁ מַבּוּל בַּחוּץ, אַל תֵּצֵא בְּלִי מְעִיל.
Example (translit): Yesh mabul ba-chutz, al tetze bli me'il.
Example (English): It's pouring outside, don't go out without a coat.

Mnemonic: ka-DOOR — kadur is also a pill and a bullet — anything small and round. Kadur ha-aretz = the globe; kaduregel = soccer.
Example (English): The children play with a ball in the park.

Mnemonic: psan-TER — from the Greek "psalterion", the same ancestor as "psalm" and "psaltery".
Example (English): There's an old piano in the living room.

Mnemonic: sar-TAN — like English, the animal and the disease share a name (Latin "cancer" = crab). Also the zodiac sign Cancer.
Example (English): We saw a small crab on the beach.

Mnemonic: ba-TOO-ach — from betach, "sure!" (a very common Israeli "of course"). It means both "safe" and "certain": Ani betucha = I'm sure.
Example (English): This place is safe for children.

Mnemonic: me-su-KAN — from sakana, danger. Note: mesukan can also mean "in danger" or, for a person, "pitiable".
Example (English): It's dangerous to swim here.

Mnemonic: cha-ZAK — "Chazak ve-ematz" = "Be strong and courageous". Same root as lehachzik, to hold on.
Example (English): The wind is very strong today.

Mnemonic: cha-LASH — a weak, LASHED-out feeling. Slang: "chalash" alone means "lame / weak sauce".
Example (English): The signal here is weak.

Mnemonic: tip-SHEE — from tipesh, a fool. Tipshi describes a thing (a stupid idea); tipesh describes a person.
Example (English): That was a stupid idea.

Mnemonic: LO-vesh — you put on a LOVELY VEST. Levush = attire; malbush = a garment.
Example (English): I wear a white shirt to work.

Mnemonic: no-EL — na'al = shoe. Hebrew uses a different verb for footwear than for clothes. (Same root also means "to lock" — a shoe closes your foot.)
Example (English): He wears black shoes.

Mnemonic: GAR — "Where do you GARage yourself?" This is where you live; it's not the verb for being alive.
Example (English): Where do you live?

Mnemonic: mish-ta-MESH — you use a tool until it's a MESH. Shimush = usage; always followed by be-.
Example (English): I use the computer for work.

Mnemonic: ma-a-DEEF — the preferred one has the ADvantage — a DIFference in your favor.
Example (English): I prefer tea over coffee.

Mnemonic: sho-LE-ach — a shaliach is a messenger, one who is SENT. "Show, LAUNCH it."
Example (English): I'm sending you a message.

Mnemonic: mar-EH — ro'eh = see, mar'eh = cause to see = show. Mar'a also means "mirror".
Example (English): Show me the pictures from the trip.

Mnemonic: cho-TEM — a chotemet is a rubber stamp. You sign or stamp to seal it.
Example (English): Sign here, please.

Mnemonic: me-na-SEH — trying is a NUISANCE until it works. Nisayon = an attempt (and "experience").
Example (English): I'm trying to understand the grammar.

Front (English): To interpret / to explain the meaning
Mnemonic: me-fa-RESH — Rashi, the great biblical commentator, is the parshan par excellence. Parasha = a portion/interpretation.
Example (Hebrew): כָּל אֶחָד מְפָרֵשׁ אֶת זֶה אַחֶרֶת.
Example (translit): Kol echad mefaresh et ze acheret.
Example (English): Everyone interprets it differently.

Mnemonic: no-FEL — "NO! FELL!" Nefila = a fall.
Example (English): The leaves fall in autumn.

Mnemonic: po-GEH-a — a POKE that hurts. Pgi'a = an injury or an offense — it covers hurting feelings too.
Example (English): His words hurt me.

Mnemonic: bo-RE-ach — "BOLT, ROACH!" — a cockroach scurrying off when the light goes on.
Example (English): The cat runs away from the dog.

Mnemonic: no-VEH-ach — it even sounds like a dog: "no-VACH! no-VACH!"
Example (English): The dog barks at every person.

Mnemonic: BO-heh — a blank, BORED "boh…" while you gaze into nothing.
Example (English): He's been staring at the wall for a while.

Mnemonic: oh-ZEV — "Azov oti!" = "Leave me alone!" One of the most-heard phrases in Israel.
Example (English): She leaves work at six.

Front (English): To pass / to cross / to move house
Mnemonic: oh-VER — you go OVER to the other side. Avar = the past (what has passed); Ivrit = Hebrew, the language of those who crossed over.
Example (English): Time passes quickly.

Mnemonic: TSO-feh — a tzofe is a scout/lookout. Use this for screens; mistakel is for looking at things.
Example (English): We're watching a movie tonight.

Mnemonic: me-ka-DESH — kadosh = holy; Kiddush is the Friday-night blessing over wine. Same root: k-d-sh.
Example (Hebrew): אַבָּא מְקַדֵּשׁ עַל הַיַּיִן בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת.
Example (translit): Aba mekadesh al ha-yayin be-erev shabbat.
Example (English): Dad makes kiddush over the wine on Friday night.

Mnemonic: na-KEE — from lenakot, to clean. Nikayon = cleaning.
Example (English): The room is clean now.

Mnemonic: me-luch-LACH — a satisfyingly grubby-sounding word. From lichluch, dirt.
Example (English): The shoes are dirty from the hike.

Mnemonic: tsiv-o-NEE — from tzeva (color). The -oni ending turns nouns into adjectives, like tzimchoni (vegetarian) from tzemach (plant).
Example (English): The market is colorful and noisy.

Mnemonic: a-FOR — from efer, "ash". Grey is ash-colored.
Example (English): The sky is grey today.

Mnemonic: mu-GAZ — literally "gassed". Mayim mugazim = sparkling water. Ask for it this way in any café.
Example (English): Could I have sparkling water, please?

Mnemonic: tsim-cho-NEE — from tzemach, "a plant". A plant-person.
Example (Hebrew): אֲנִי צִמְחוֹנִית, יֵשׁ מָנָה בְּלִי בָּשָׂר?
Example (translit): Ani tzimchonit, yesh mana bli basar?
Example (English): I'm vegetarian, is there a dish without meat?

Mnemonic: tiv-o-NEE — from teva, "nature". Israel has one of the highest vegan rates in the world, so you'll hear it often.
Example (English): This restaurant is entirely vegan.

Mnemonic: me-uch-ZAV — from achzava, disappointment, built on kazav, "a lie": you were let down by a false hope.
Example (English): I'm disappointed by the movie.

Mnemonic: kol kach — literally "all thus". "Kol kach yafe!" = "So beautiful!" It goes before the adjective.
Example (English): The food was so tasty!

Mnemonic: KVAR — Israelis use kvar for impatience too: "Bo kvar!" = "Come on already!"
Example (English): I already ate, thanks.

Mnemonic: KOL — with "the" it means all (kol ha-yom = all day); without it, every (kol yom = every day). One tiny word, two meanings.
Example (Hebrew): אֲנִי לוֹמֶדֶת כָּל יוֹם, לֹא כָּל הַיּוֹם.
Example (translit): Ani lomedet kol yom, lo kol ha-yom.
Example (English): I study every day, not all day.

Mnemonic: har-BEH — a HERD of things. Doesn't change for gender or number — one form fits all.
Example (English): I have a lot of work this week.

Mnemonic: ha-MON — originally "a crowd, a multitude". Stronger than harbeh: "Toda hamon!" = "Thanks a million!"
Example (English): There were a ton of people there.

Mnemonic: Literally "it doesn't change" — from leshanot, to change. One of the most useful throwaway phrases in Hebrew.
Example (Hebrew): לֹא מְשַׁנֶּה, נַעֲשֶׂה אֶת זֶה מָחָר.
Example (translit): Lo meshane, ne'ase et ze machar.
Example (English): Never mind, we'll do it tomorrow.

Mnemonic: ETS-li — from etzel, "at/by". It takes endings for every person: etzli, etzlecha, etzlo, etzla. "Ba'im etzli?" = "Coming to my place?"
Example (English): Dinner is at my place tonight.

Mnemonic: EH-leh — the plural of ze/zo (this). Ha-sfarim ha-ele = "these books" (Hebrew repeats the "ha-").
Example (English): These flowers are for you.

Mnemonic: Standing alone you say shnayim / shtayim; but right before a noun they shorten to shnei (m.) / shtei (f.). Shnei sfarim, shtei banot.
Example (English): I bought two glasses and two plates.

Mnemonic: ha-YA — the past tense of "to be", the verb that vanishes in the present. Haya cham = "it was hot". You'll meet its full conjugation in Phase 2.
Example (English): The movie was very interesting.

Mnemonic: Same word as the verb "can" — Hebrew uses it like an adjective, followed by an infinitive: Ani yachol lalechet. Note it changes for gender, like an adjective.
Example (English): We can help you.
